caseno: Death reference 1 of 1986 with Jail Appeal No. 6 of 1986.
lawyer:
Shawkat Ali Khan with Fazlul Huq Khan and Md. Tamizuddin, Advocates ------ For the condemned prisoner.
M Moazzam Hossain, Deputy Attorney-General ------ For the State.
parties:
Abdur Rahman Syed ------ Appellant 
Vs. 
State ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
51. Mr. Shawkat Ali Khan submits that the statement of the accused recorded under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not only the result of torture but also recorded not in accordance with law. We have examined this point also and having examined the statement under section 164 CrPC we find that it is recorded in a printed form and we also find that the main printed form was missing from the original records of the case which is not explained but a photo copy of the same was found in the police records. On an examination of the said photo copy we find that the learned Magistrate did ask him the reasons for his confession and he said that he is repentant and thus making the statement and the Magistrate gave him all the caution as required under law as clearly stated by the Magistrate as a witness. After the recording, the Magistrate gave a certificate that this confession he believed to be voluntary and made in his presence and he read over the statements to the maker and the person making it admitted it to be correct. This recording of the Magistrate in his official capacity and the certificate given by him as such has some legal presumption of its due performance under section 114 of the Evidence Act and the person alleging otherwise needs to prove it. In the instant case except a vague suggestion that it was not properly recorded there is nothing to substantiate or even to make it probable. This allegation of torture that one of his legs had been broken by the police is a very serious allegation and if he was so beaten or his leg broken or hot water poured on his face by the police it ought to have been found by the Magistrate immediately after he made the confessional statement or after he was taken from police custody but no such mark or injuries had been found on the body of the maker of the confession by the Magistrate and the Magistrate PW 17 clearly stated that the confessing accused did not tell him of any ill behaviour by the police and no police was nearby and after examination he did not find any mark of injury on the person of the maker of the confession. He had not complained of any such torture but on the contrary he made the statement claiming that he is doing so being repentant and on that he has given a certificate to the effect that he believed the statements to be voluntary. This unsubstantiated allegation of torture made at a very belated stage during the cross-examination is not also in conformity with the statement of the accused made under section 342 CrPC because there the accused himself did not allege that his leg was broken or hot water was poured over his face. These are therefore, nothing but wild allegation having no basis. An allegations of torture ought to have been made at the earliest possible opportunity and an unsubstantiated and self contradicted allegation of police torture would not warrant an interference with the finding of fact arrived at by the Magistrate after examining the accused in person and after hearing the reply of the accused in person that the confessional statement was voluntary BCR 104, PLD 1964 (SC) 2161 when in fact it has been the consistent view of the courts of this sub-continent that a confession which is voluntary, even if retracted later, could be the sole basis for a conviction [Ref. PLD 1964 (SC) 413, 31 DLR 312, 16 DLR (Dhaka) 598 and 32 DLR 227). 

 Muhammad Ansar Ali J: I have heard the judgment just delivered by my learned brother and I fully concur with the same but in doing so I like to add a few lines of mine for my own satisfaction. It is a case of murder. Admittedly there is no eye-witness of the actual occurrence of causing death to the victim. The conviction of the condemned prisoner has been based solely on circumstantial evidence as well as on his self-inculpatory confession made before PW 17, the Magistrate. It is well-settled that self inculpatory confession of an accused may be alone sufficient for his, conviction, if it is found to be voluntary, true and trustworthy. But before convicting the accused on the sole basis of such confession, it is a rule of prudence and caution, though not of law that the said confession is corroborated by some other evidence on record, particularly when there is a subsequent retraction of such confession. The corroboration of course may even come from the recovery of some incriminating articles recovered at the showing of the accused. It has also to be seen that in recording the confession of the accused, the recording Magistrate has fully complied with the provisions of section 164, particularly sub-section 3 of section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and he is fully satisfied by making a real and substantial inquiry by eliciting answers to some material questions put to the accused to be sure that the accused in his own volition and without any inducement, threat, torture, promise or allurement from any quarter is wanting to make the confession. It is of course not necessary that each and every circumstances appearing in the confession needs be corroborated separately and independently. The above principles have been enunciated in a number of a decisions of the Superior courts of the Subcontinent and few of them are reported in 32 DLR 227 (Salauddin Vs. State), 1981 BCR 104 (Shefali Begum and another Vs. State, PLD 1964 SC 216 (Qibla Alam Vs. State), 1971 SC MR 341, AIR 1957 SC 216 (Balabir Singh Vs. State of Punjab). In the instant case in the light of the above settled principles of law, if the confessional statement of the accused is read and scrutinized, it will be found that the facts and circumstances of the case about the commission of the murder of the victim by the condemned prisoner as appearing in his self inculpatory confession do get enough corroboration from the materials on record. So far the truth and voluntariness of the said confession are concerned, it appears that the recording Magistrate PW 17 Kazi Md. Rafiquzzaman has been examined and cross examined in this case and he has categorically stated that the accused Abdur Rahman being repentant voluntarily made the confessional statement before him under section 164 CrPC on 17.2.85 and no mark of any injury or torture was found on any part of the body of the accused appellant even after due inspection and there was also no allegation of any torture, allurement or inducement by the confessing accused. Besides PW 17 the recording Magistrate flatly denied a suggestion that the accused did not make any confession voluntarily. Further, it appears on scrutiny of the confessional statement that before recording the same, sufficient time was given to the accused for his reflection and then several necessary questions 'were put to him and answers thereto were obtained by the recording Magistrate for testing the voluntariness of the confessional statement of the maker thereof. The recording Magistrate testified to the effect that the inculpatory confession made by the accused Abdur Rahman was voluntary and true. The learned Sessions Judge duly considered the confessional statement and on scrutiny found the same to be voluntary and true and the alleged retraction of the same to be false and a belated one. Apart from that the confession as recorded by the Magistrate naturally gives rise to a presumption of genuineness under section 114(e) of the Evidence Act and the said presumption does not appear to have been sufficiently rebutted by the defence by any reliable evidence. The contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant condemned prisoner is that the alleged confession was made on 17.2.85 whereas according to the prosecution the alleged occurrence has taken place on 10.2.85 and when the matter first came up in the newspaper on 13.2.85, the FIR was lodged by the informant PW 1 on 14.2.85 and as such police had occasion and sufficient time to torture and tutor the accused to make the said confession which was neither voluntary nor true. We have carefully considered the above contentions of the learned Advocate for the appellant vis-a-vis the evidence on record and we have found no substance in same. The so-called retraction though suggested by the defence while cross examining the witnesses and examining the accused under section 342 CrPC appears to have no reliable basis to stand upon. Hence, the alleged retraction goes unsubstantiated in the facts and circumstances of the case and it clearly appears that the provisions of section 164 CrPC as required under the law have been fully complied with by the recording Magistrate and the self-inculpatory confession of the condemned prisoner appears to be quite true, voluntary and trustworthy and hence this could rightly be relied upon as the sole basis for his conviction.
